title: Seven Questions to Ask Before Joining a Concierge Practice
description: A seven-question checklist for physicians weighing a concierge role, set against the 2027 Medicare fee schedule and what a quarter century of payment decline actually produced.
excerpt: The recruiting call is sound in its premise and oversold in its conclusion. Seven questions that get at the parts of an arrangement that are hard to renegotiate once you have started.
author: Blue Angel Journal
intro: CMS – the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the federal agency that sets what Medicare pays for each service – finalized its 2027 physician payment rules on November 4th. As a reminder of how the arithmetic works: Medicare prices a service by multiplying the value it assigns that service by a single dollar figure called the conversion factor, which means one number moves every fee at once. For 2027 it falls to $32.63 for most clinicians, down 2.31% from $33.40, and to $32.95 for those in qualifying alternative payment models, down 1.83% from $33.57. Both came in slightly deeper than what CMS proposed back in July – $32.84 and $33.17 – largely because a work relative value unit adjustment moved from plus 0.53% in the proposal to minus 0.12% in the final rule. The changes take effect January 1st.
takeaways: The 2027 conversion factor falls 2.31 percent for most clinicians, but the sequence matters more than any single year.
Physician-owned practice fell from 60.1 percent in 2012 to 42.2 percent in 2024, and nearly all of that went to employment rather than independence.
Membership medicine accounts for under 2 percent of US physicians by trade estimates, so it is one job at one practice rather than a structural answer.
Ask for three documents before the second conversation: the membership agreement, last year's real coverage schedule, and the compensation structure with its downside case.

sections.title: Why the call is coming now
paragraphs: Two percent on its own is not a reason to change jobs. The sequence is. The American Medical Association calculates that Medicare physician payment declined 33% between 2001 and 2025 once inflation is accounted for. That is an advocacy organization's own analysis and should be read as one – but the mechanism behind it is dull and hard to argue with: the fee schedule carries no automatic inflation adjustment, so a year with no increase is a cut, and most years have had no increase. John Corker, M.D., an emergency physician and an Ohio State Medical Association delegate, put it to the AMA as practices "dying a slow death by a thousand paper cuts" on reimbursement. That is the backdrop against which someone is about to describe a membership practice's economics to you.

So it is worth asking what a quarter century of that actually produced, because the answer is not quite what the pitch implies. The AMA's benchmark survey put 42.2% of physicians in wholly physician-owned practices in 2024, down from 60.1% in 2012 – and nearly all of that difference went to employment rather than to independence. Membership medicine absorbed a sliver: Concierge Medicine Today estimates that under 2% of US physicians work in a subscription or membership practice, and describes its own figures as directional rather than precise, since no federal registry tracks them. In other words, the squeeze is real and it is not ending, but a model that 2% of physicians have moved to is not a structural answer to a structural problem. It is one job at one practice, and it has to be good on those terms rather than on the strength of what you would be leaving.
What follows are seven questions that get at the parts of an arrangement that are hard to renegotiate once you have started. They are ordered roughly by how expensive the wrong answer is.

sections.title: How large is the panel, and how is that number counted?
paragraphs: Panel size is the number every practice leads with, and it is the one most worth pinning down. Ask how many members there are today rather than how many the practice is built for, and ask whether that count is members or households – a practice counting households can have half again as many people calling. Ask whether you will also see patients who are not members, and how that gets billed. Then ask what the number is meant to be in two years, because a panel of 300 intended to stay at 300 is a different job from a panel of 300 on its way to 600, and the second version is the one that quietly rewrites your schedule. Staffing is the check on any panel figure: writing in Medical Economics, a former practice manager at Specialdocs suggested roughly 2.5 staff for every 250 to 300 patients. That is a vendor's guidance rather than an industry standard, but it gives you a ratio to hold against what the practice actually employs – and where the staffing is thinner and the panel larger, the difference tends to arrive as work for the physician.

sections.title: What has the practice promised its members in writing?
paragraphs: Ask to read the membership agreement before your second conversation. As the October 27 issue argued, a practice is whatever its agreement says rather than whatever the word concierge implies, which is exactly why this is the document that tells you what the job is. It is a reasonable request, and a practice that will not show it has told you something. What you are looking for is the list of commitments that become yours: how quickly a member can expect an appointment, how messages get answered and within what window, whether a number reaches you directly, what happens at a weekend, and which services sit inside the fee rather than beside it. The American Medical Association's opinion on retainer practices asks physicians to set those terms out plainly, keep participation voluntary, avoid implying that the retainer buys better medical care, and bill retainer charges separately from services covered by insurance – a serviceable standard to read any agreement against. Check the insurance structure in the same pass, since the Academy of Family Physicians describes direct primary care as a periodic fee for defined primary care services without billing insurance for them, while concierge practices often combine a membership fee with insurance billing, and Medicare does not cover the membership fee under either. A vague agreement is not a lighter obligation. It is an obligation whose limits get decided later, usually while a patient is unhappy.

sections.title: Who covers the panel when you are away?
paragraphs: Access promises fail first on vacations, illness and conferences, so ask for last year's actual coverage schedule rather than the coverage policy. Who answered calls in July? What did members hear when they rang? Could the covering clinician open a chart and prescribe, or only reassure? Ask it in the other direction too – how often will you cover for someone else, and is that time reflected anywhere in your schedule or your compensation? In a two or three physician practice, reciprocal coverage is a substantial part of the job and it is almost never in the offer letter. The honest version of this question is not whether coverage exists, because it always does on paper. It is whether the person covering can do the specific thing a member will need on the specific day they need it.

sections.title: Which decisions are yours?
paragraphs: Independent practice and clinical autonomy are not the same thing, and a practice can offer one without the other. Ask which decisions sit with you: panel composition, appointment length, how many patients you see in a day, referral patterns, which labs and imaging the practice uses, and whether you can decline a membership request. Then ask how those decisions are documented, because a verbal assurance from a founding physician is worth something only for as long as that physician is there. If the practice has management support, a partner organization or outside ownership, ask plainly where clinical judgment stops being yours and ask for the answer in writing. The distinction that matters is between an arrangement that supports the practice and one that directs the medicine – and the agreement, rather than the conversation, is where that line actually sits.

sections.title: Who does the business work?
paragraphs: Physicians moving out of employment consistently report that the business side is harder than expected. In the same Medical Economics discussion, a physician who left hospital employment described accounting, legal work, human resources and information technology as the most overwhelming part of the change, and the Specialdocs representatives estimated roughly three months to transition an independent practice and up to six months for someone leaving an employed role. So ask who owns each function today: membership billing and collections, payroll, vendor contracts, the electronic health record, credentialing, marketing and the website. Ask who answers when a member's payment fails. Membership billing deserves a direct question, because in a membership practice it is the revenue cycle rather than an administrative detail. And if there is an operational partner, ask what it does and – more usefully – what it does not do. BACP's own description of practice support shows where one partner draws that line. Then ask to speak with a physician who has worked under that arrangement for more than a year.

sections.title: How are you paid, and what happens if membership revenue moves?
paragraphs: Ask for the structure, then ask for the downside case. Salary, a share of membership revenue, a share of collections, or some combination? If membership revenue falls because members leave or the fee stays flat, what absorbs it – the practice, or your pay? If the panel grows, does your compensation grow with it, or does the growth accrue elsewhere while the work accrues to you? Ask what the fee is now, when it was last raised, and who decides the next increase, because fee decisions shape both your income and your panel, and in most practices the owner makes them alone. Unfortunately this is the question candidates most often accept a general answer to, and a general answer here is the one that costs the most later.

sections.title: What happens to the patients if you leave?
paragraphs: This is the question candidates skip and later regret. Ask what the agreement says about notice, non-competition and non-solicitation, who holds the medical records, and who tells the members. There is a professional obligation sitting underneath the contract terms: the AMA's guidance on ending a patient relationship asks a physician withdrawing from a case to give notice far enough ahead for the patient to find another physician, and to help transfer care. Find out now how the practice would make that possible, because a restrictive covenant drafted without it puts you somewhere you do not want to be later. The time to discover that conflict is before you sign, not when you are trying to leave.

sections.title: Two things that changed in 2026 and bear on the answer
paragraphs: The first is a payment change that took effect at the start of this year. Under Notice 2026-05, issued on December 9th 2025, an otherwise eligible individual enrolled in certain direct primary care arrangements may contribute to a health savings account and may use HSA funds to pay the periodic fee. Benefits advisers summarizing the notice report conditions on what qualifies – including a monthly cap and a requirement that the arrangement cover only primary care – though the IRS newsroom summary states no figures, so confirm the detail in the notice itself. Importantly, a concierge practice that bills insurance for primary care generally falls outside the direct primary care definition, which means the new treatment may not reach it at all. If a practice offers the rule change as evidence that its membership will grow, that is a claim worth asking it to substantiate.

The second is that the reporting regime you might be leaving now has its own published end date. The same final rule sets traditional MIPS reporting to end after the 2031 performance period, gives clinicians through 2030 to move to MIPS Value Pathways or advanced alternative payment models, and requires at least one specialty-specific core measure from 2027. The honest takeaway is that if part of the appeal of a membership practice is getting out from under MIPS, the escape now has a timetable of its own – and a practice that still bills Medicare will be inside whatever replaces it.

sections.title: The takeaway
paragraphs: Ask for three documents before the second conversation: the membership agreement, last year's real coverage schedule, and the compensation structure with its downside case. A practice that can hand you all three has thought about the job it is offering. A practice that cannot has not finished deciding what that job is, and you would end up deciding it for them without the authority to do so. And separate the two questions that the timing invites you to merge – whether Medicare payment is getting harder was answered on November 4th, and whether this particular practice is a good place to work is a different question that nothing in the fee schedule touches.

faqs.question: Is the 2027 fee schedule a reason to leave an employed role?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. The conversion factor falls 2.31 percent for most clinicians and 1.83 percent for those in qualifying alternative payment models, which is not why anyone changes jobs. The sequence is the argument: the fee schedule carries no automatic inflation adjustment, so a flat year is a cut, and most years have been flat.

faqs.question: What should I ask for before a second conversation with a practice?
faqs.answer: Three documents. The membership agreement, because its promises become yours. Last year's actual coverage schedule rather than the coverage policy. And the compensation structure with its downside case, including what happens if membership revenue falls.

faqs.question: Does joining a concierge practice mean leaving MIPS behind?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, and the escape now has a timetable of its own. The same final rule sets traditional MIPS reporting to end after the 2031 performance period and gives clinicians through 2030 to move to MIPS Value Pathways or advanced alternative payment models. A practice that still bills Medicare will be inside whatever replaces it.
